source.title: Association of Sprint Performance With Ground Reaction Forces During Acceleration and Maximal Speed Phases in a Single Sprint

paper.citation: Nagahara, R., Mizutani, M., Matsuo, A., Kanehisa, H., & Fukunaga, T. (2018). Association of sprint performance with ground reaction forces during acceleration and maximal speed phases in a single sprint. Journal of Applied Biomechanics, 34(2), 104–110. https://doi.org/10.1123/jab.2016-0356
paper.abstract: Which ground-reaction-force variables are associated with acceleration at different relative speeds and with maximal running speed? Eighteen male university-club athletes, age 20.6 ± 1.2 years, 100-m best 10.54–12.30 s. Maximal 60-m block-start sprint in spikes on a 54-force-platform runway. Track-sprint context; transfer to collegiate American-football starts and field surfaces is indirect. Cross-sectional analysis of each athlete's fastest of two to five sprints. GRF collected at 1,000 Hz through 50.5 m and summarized as impulses and mean forces. Stepwise multiple regression selected candidate contributors, which can be unstable in a small sample.
paper.tldr: This paper informs phase-specific interpretation of propulsive, braking, and vertical forces during sprinting. Greater propulsive impulse contributed to higher acceleration across 55–95% of maximal speed, while smaller braking impulse contributed across 75–95%. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional analysis of each athlete's fastest of two to five sprints. GRF collected at 1,000 Hz through 50.5 m and summarized as impulses and mean forces. Stepwise multiple regression selected candidate contributors, which can be unstable in a small sample.
paper.findings: Greater propulsive impulse contributed to higher acceleration across 55–95% of maximal speed, while smaller braking impulse contributed across 75–95%. Greater mean vertical force was selected as a contributor to maximal running speed. Vertical impulse was unchanged across acceleration even as mean vertical force rose with speed, illustrating that force magnitude and impulse are not interchangeable.
paper.limitations: The 95%-maximal-speed point averaged 23.1 m, shorter than the authors' expected full acceleration phase above 40 m. Standardizing athletes by percentage of maximal speed introduces alignment bias. The performance range was not world-class, and the small sample plus stepwise regression limits model stability. Association does not prove that cueing force changes will improve sprint performance.
paper.practicalImplications: Use these force patterns as descriptive mechanical targets, then confirm them against actual sprint splits. In collegiate American football, task, start position, surface, equipment, and acceleration distance should be matched before applying the phase labels.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. Use these force patterns as descriptive mechanical targets, then confirm them against actual sprint splits. In collegiate American football, task, start position, surface, equipment, and acceleration distance should be matched before applying the phase labels. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: This study did not directly evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. It provides no standalone clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-play progression.
